content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a severe genetic disorder caused by the inheritance of two abnormal beta-globin genes. It is associated with significant complications, including severe pain, organ damage, pulmonary issues, and premature death. Silent cerebral infarcts (SCIs) are the most common neurological complication in children with SCD and likely in adults as well. These infarcts can impair academic performance, exacerbate cognitive deficits, and lower intelligence quotient (IQ). The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions aimed at reducing or preventing SCIs in individuals with SCD. The analysis included five randomized controlled trials conducted between 1998 and 2016, involving a total of 660 children or adolescents. Most participants had the HbSS form of SCD. Four of the five trials were terminated early, and the quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low due to methodological limitations, including high risk of bias, indirectness of evidence, and imprecise outcome estimates. Long-term red blood cell transfusions versus standard care: 1. Children with abnormal transcranial Doppler (TCD) velocities or a history of SCIs: Long-term red blood cell transfusions may reduce the incidence of SCIs in children with abnormal TCD velocities (risk ratio [RR] 0.11, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 0.86; low-quality evidence). However, transfusions may have little or no effect on the incidence of SCIs in children with a history of SCIs and normal or conditional TCD velocities (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.23 to 2.13; low-quality evidence). No deaths were reported in either trial. 2. Other outcomes: Long-term transfusions may reduce the incidence of acute chest syndrome (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.49; low-quality evidence) and painful crises (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95; low-quality evidence). Transfusions probably reduce the risk of clinical stroke (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.49; moderate-quality evidence). Transfusions may improve quality of life in children with prior SCIs (difference estimate -0.54, 95% CI -0.92 to -0.17; low-quality evidence) but may have no effect on cognitive function (least squares means: 1.7, 95% CI -1.1 to 4.4; low-quality evidence). Continuing transfusions versus stopping transfusions in children and adolescents with normalized TCD velocities: Continuing transfusions may reduce the incidence of SCIs (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.97; low-quality evidence). The effect of continuing transfusions on all-cause mortality (Peto odds ratio [OR] 8.00, 95% CI 0.16 to 404.12) and clinical stroke (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.35) is very uncertain (very low-quality evidence). This trial did not report data on SCD-related adverse events, quality of life, or cognitive function. Hydroxyurea and phlebotomy versus transfusions and chelation therapy: 1. Primary prevention in children: There is very low-quality evidence regarding the effects of switching to hydroxyurea and phlebotomy on SCIs (no infarcts reported), all-cause mortality (no deaths), stroke risk (no strokes), or SCD-related complications (RR 1.52, 95% CI 0.58 to 4.02). 2. Secondary prevention in children and adolescents with a history of stroke: The effect of switching to hydroxyurea and phlebotomy on SCIs (Peto OR 7.28, 95% CI 0.14 to 366.91), all-cause mortality (Peto OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.06 to 16.41), and clinical stroke (RR 14.78, 95% CI 0.86 to 253.66) is very uncertain (very low-quality evidence). Switching to hydroxyurea and phlebotomy may increase the risk of SCD-related complications (RR 3.10, 95% CI 1.42 to 6.75; low-quality evidence). Neither trial reported data on quality of life or cognitive function. Authors' conclusions: No trials were identified for preventing SCIs in adults or in children without HbSS SCD. Long-term red blood cell transfusions may reduce the incidence of SCIs in children with abnormal TCD velocities but may have little or no effect in children with normal TCD velocities. In children at higher risk of stroke who have not previously received long-term transfusions, transfusions probably reduce the risk of stroke and other SCD-related complications, such as acute chest syndrome and painful crises. In children and adolescents with normalized TCD velocities, continuing transfusions may reduce the risk of SCIs. However, no clear threshold for stopping transfusions has been established. Switching to hydroxyurea and phlebotomy may increase the risk of SCIs and SCD-related serious adverse events in secondary stroke prevention. Overall, the quality of evidence for most outcomes is very low, highlighting the need for further high-quality research.
